\chapter{Introduction}
\section{Service Discovery and Authorized Invocation}
Named Data Networking (NDN) supports name-based Data retrieval and data-centric security~\cite{ndn,ndnpacket}.
Applications can use a trust schema to specify which signing keys are authorized to sign which Data and guide Data validation~\cite{trustschema}.
Sync announces dataset changes so applications can retrieve available Data~\cite{li2018brief,moll2022sok}.
These building blocks do not, by themselves, select a service executor or guarantee completion before a deadline; invocation authorization requires application-specific rules and checks.
A requester may know the required service without knowing which authorized Providers are currently reachable, capable, and willing to execute it.
Even when one Provider suffices, candidate discovery, authorization, selection, and result retrieval remain application responsibilities.
NFN, NFaaS, RICE, and NSC support named computation or invocation~\cite{nfn,nfaas,rice,nsc}.
The Distributed Network Measurement Protocol (DNMP) provides a concrete example of Trust-Schema-based command authorization~\cite{dnmp}.
These NDN systems provide the computation, invocation, and authorization precedents against which this proposal examines NDNSF's design choices.
\section{The Initial NDNSF Foundation}
The initial NDNSF prototype selects one Provider from multiple candidates for each invocation.
The User publishes Request Data, collects acknowledgment (ACK) Data, and publishes Selection Data for the chosen Provider, which executes and publishes Response Data.
Candidates offer alternatives for the same invocation; the initial prototype does not assign them to different, interdependent roles.
Discovery and authorization remain research subjects independently of collaboration.
A discovery descriptor supplies feasibility information, such as deadlines and resource requirements; application input supplies execution material.
In the evaluated design, attribute-based encryption (ABE) protects descriptors, while protected-challenge verification, signatures under trust rules, and request-state checks govern authorization.
Authorized but unselected candidates can read descriptors.
The study also evaluates input/result protection, permission grants and withdrawals, and management costs.
\section{Extending Invocation to Multi-Provider Collaboration}
Some tasks require complementary services from different Providers.
Independently invoking each service does not by itself specify which Provider fills each role or which intermediate objects a dependent service may accept.
This proposal investigates an extension that makes those assignments and dependencies explicit while retaining the invocation foundation.
For example, nearby unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) could collect different views of a ground area for analysis by a compute Provider.
The extension would assign sensing and processing roles and check each image against its declared dependency.
Area and deadline information may be needed before ACK to assess feasibility; processing images can be disclosed through Selection.
Descriptor encryption limits reading to authorized candidates, not exposure of names or traffic patterns.
This case motivates the extension; recognition algorithms remain an application choice.
\section{Thesis and Research Questions}

The thesis to be evaluated is that named, verifiable objects can support runtime service discovery and authorized single-Provider invocation, and that explicit role and dependency rules can extend this foundation to multi-Provider tasks.
The study evaluates the discovery/authorization design and the collaboration extension separately.
Benefits must justify their discovery, validation, communication, and key-management costs under the tested conditions.

\item How can NDNSF discover willing Providers while keeping discovery descriptors confidential from unauthorized readers and checking service permissions before execution, and at what cost relative to complete alternative designs?

\item How can the single-Provider invocation foundation be extended so Providers selected at runtime follow task roles and named dependencies, whether intermediate Data is retrieved from producers or caches?
\item Under what workload and network conditions do these mechanisms improve completion, latency, or execution efficiency, and when do their costs outweigh their benefits?
RQ1 evaluates the invocation foundation, including a DNMP-inspired role-authorization alternative paired with content encryption and adapted to the NDNSF workflow.
RQ2 investigates the collaboration extension through UAV and distributed-inference dependencies; RQ3 measures both scopes and their applicable failure behavior separately.
\section{Contribution and Evidence Boundary}

The intended contributions are an evaluated discovery/authorization design, a collaboration protocol enforcing runtime role assignments through named-dependency checks, and evidence of their benefits and costs.
These build on established NDN, encryption, and computation mechanisms.
Existing invocation experiments do not validate a multi-role plan.
The extension adds role and dependency rules without replacing existing request-ID isolation.
Later implementation work is not attributed to the initial prototype; collaboration end-to-end evaluation remains incomplete.
Chapter~\ref{chap:evaluation} separates available findings from required evidence.
\chapter{Related Work and Design Alternatives}
\section{Named Computation, Invocation, and Composition}
NFN studies named computation and expression evaluation; NFaaS studies execution placement in a named-function environment~\cite{nfn,nfaas}.
RICE provides an invocation handshake with support for authentication and security information~\cite{rice}.
NSC specifies signed invocation Interests validated using an application-provided Trust Schema, and discusses protected input and result exchange~\cite{nsc}.
These designs establish relevant invocation and authorization mechanisms.
Experimental comparisons below refer to the tested NSC configuration, not every feature of its full design.

For the collaboration extension, the question is how a request gathers current willingness and feasibility information before assigning execution roles, and how that assignment constrains intermediate-object use.
Long-term service permission does not identify the Provider assigned to a particular predecessor role.
Neither a request ID nor a valid signature alone expresses that assignment.
The proposed contribution is the enforced connection between runtime assignment and object use, rather than the manifest format itself.

Service-composition work such as CaSCON~\cite{cascon} is a relevant comparator; the research will examine assignment timing, dependency validation, and recovery semantics alongside workflow-security and capability-based designs.
Novelty beyond this proposed scope remains to be established by that comparison.

\subsection{Adapting the Alternative to NDNSF}
For comparison, we propose retaining the NDNSF Request--ACK--Selection--Response workflow while replacing ABE-backed invocation checks with role-constrained signing rules.
The alternative must authorize both User invocation and Provider participation, match messages to active requests, and permit execution only after Selection.
These adaptations are not features attributed to DNMP itself.
Both designs require descriptor confidentiality before selection, recipient-scoped input/result protection afterward, and checks for withdrawn authority.

Role granularity is policy-defined: a role can cover multiple actions, and credentials can be reused where the rules permit.
DNMP is therefore a concrete authorization precedent, not evidence that every service needs a new signing certificate.
This comparison concerns complete designs, not measured DNMP-versus-NDNSF performance.
The invocation-state and encryption choices must be implemented and evaluated under matched requirements before claiming a cost advantage.
Recipient encryption protects selected exchanges; service-group encryption or ABE can protect discovery before participants are selected.
Trust Schema alone does not provide confidentiality, but it can be combined with either mechanism.
The proposed alternative requires current revocation-status checks or certificate expiry.
Deleting a certificate from a repository does not invalidate cached copies.
We do not attribute NDNSF's runtime revocation protocol to DNMP.
\section{Protected Discovery and Permission Management}
NDNSF uses ABE for two related purposes: protecting discovery descriptors before Provider selection and managing service permissions independently of identity-signing credentials.
The User publishes encrypted descriptors for shared retrieval, while the Controller issues policy keys defining decryption access.
The enhanced NAC-ABE library provides KP-ABE support~\cite{dulal2023nacabe}.
NDNSF connects these permissions to invocation by checking protected challenge values, message signatures under trust rules, and current authorization/request state.
Content encryption supplies confidentiality; the combined checks govern participation and execution.
Section~\ref{sec:abe-rationale} explains the reuse of permission management and its additional costs.
The comparison must include group-key or broadcast-encryption alternatives where appropriate.
A stable, small group can make conventional group encryption attractive; known Providers and simple permissions can favor signed invocation with recipient encryption.

ABE becomes attractive when recipients are identified by service entitlement before their current identities are known, and multiple entitlements should remain independent of identity-signing credentials.
Policy size, membership churn, encryption cost, and authority availability bound this argument.
\chapter{NDNSF System Model and Protocol}
This chapter first describes the invocation and authorization design under evaluation, then introduces the proposed collaboration extension.
Later confidentiality and lifecycle refinements are not attributed to every initial-prototype path.
The basic invocation selects one Provider; role assignments and named dependency edges belong to the extension.
\section{Participants, Trust, and Exclusions}
These are protocol roles, not necessarily separate devices: one node may be both a User and a Provider.
The managed organization registers identities and approves service permissions; the Controller administers that policy.
Participants require a provisioned trust anchor and validation rules for identity certificates and Controller material.
Not knowing which candidates will respond to this invocation does not mean that the authorization authority has never enrolled those entities.
Billing, arbitrary business transactions, globally optimal scheduling, and protection against all denial-of-service traffic are outside the claimed scope.
The User requests a service and selects its Provider; in the collaboration extension, it also coordinates role assignments.
Providers offer and execute services.
A Controller administers authorization material and signed status.
Forwarders and caches can deliver Data without being trusted to authorize execution.
The model trusts the Controller and the User's planning decision; it does not claim consensus against a malicious coordinator.
An attacker may observe visible names and traffic, inject invalid objects, replay previously valid messages, or operate without the needed service permission.
Credential compromise and intentional sharing by an authorized principal require additional controls and are not prevented by ABE alone.
Authorization is permission to perform an operation, authentication establishes the signing identity under trust rules, and confidentiality limits who can recover Content.
Valid credentials do not prove honest load reports, correct inference, or truthful sensor observations.
Signed status must be obtained and validated before it can affect local authorization; a disconnected participant cannot be assumed to learn revocation immediately.
Deadline/expiry checks require an explicit clock policy.
Tests must report the allowed skew and failure behavior rather than silently assume synchronized clocks.

\section{Authorization and Confidentiality}
Discovery confidentiality applies to descriptor Content against parties lacking the required ABE decryption capability.
It does not conceal the descriptor from other authorized candidates or provide traffic-analysis resistance.

In the request-scoped protection design, the User encrypts application input with a symmetric key and delivers the necessary key material through Selection, encrypted for the chosen Provider's authenticated public key.
The response key is shared by the requesting User and selected Provider.
Other Users cannot decrypt the protected result under the key-secrecy assumptions; the Provider necessarily knows the plaintext it produces.
These are the protection requirements for the evaluated design, rather than claims about every historical implementation path.

\section{Conditional Correctness Argument}
Assume uncompromised signing keys, correctly enforced trust/authorization checks, and Providers that obey the specified state machine.
Selection-before-execution follows only if every handler-start path checks an active assignment and unspent authorization state.
Dependency integrity follows only if every input path, including a cache hit, checks the assigned producer and declared edge before satisfying the dependency.
Replacement isolation additionally requires old workers and late callbacks to lose authority under the new execution identity.
Restart recovery must preserve or safely invalidate the relevant one-time state; signature validity and cache FreshnessPeriod alone are insufficient.
These are conditional invariants and implementation proof obligations, not a cryptographic proof of a complete system.
Tests should inject a wrong-role object within the same request, an undeclared edge from a correctly signed producer, and a late callback after replacement.
Each isolates a property that a request ID alone cannot express.
Application result correctness and physical side effects remain outside this argument.

\section{NDNSF-UAV: Control, Sensing, and Collaboration}
\subsection{Application Structure and Service Workflows}
The UAV application connects an operator's ground station with drone-side service containers.
Drone services expose camera operations, telemetry, and mission-related operations through NDNSF.
The ground station can also provide an object-detection service, so the same application includes both service consumption and service provision.
Application code interprets camera, vehicle, and mission data; NDNSF supplies the reusable invocation and data-delivery mechanisms.
These operations cover different framework requirements.
Selecting a currently available sensing Provider exercises discovery and ACK-based selection.
Addressing an already chosen vehicle exercises invocation associated with that Provider rather than selecting an arbitrary substitute.

\subsection{Application Structure and Inference Workflows}
NDNSF-DI provides an inference application layer over the framework.
It interprets model and task descriptions, coordinates model preparation and execution, and exposes inference results to callers.
Its native requester and Provider interfaces include request submission, service registration, result/event handling, and cancellation; conversation-related interfaces also carry continuation state.
The presence of an interface is not evidence that every model or recovery configuration has passed end-to-end tests.
A single-Provider inference request exercises service discovery, permission checks, selection, protected input delivery, and result retrieval without requiring model partitioning.
Preparing a cold model and reusing a resident model exercise different readiness and artifact-access paths.
Model files and recorded artifacts may use managed repository storage; the forwarding Content Store remains opportunistic caching, not guaranteed persistence.
DI defines model identity, compatibility, and placement policy, while NDNSF supplies service lifecycle and named-object exchange.
Streamed inference and conversation workflows extend coverage to incremental outputs, cancellation, terminal status, and request-specific state.
Model weights, activation tensors, and key/value (K/V) state have distinct lifetimes.
The model computes K/V tensors and the inference runtime retains them for later decoding; shared buffers can avoid copying the whole cache at each step~\cite{ortkvcache}.
Resident weights do not replace this state.
DI owns tokenization and KV compatibility rules; framework validation concerns the authorized request, data exchange, and lifecycle through which the application uses that state.
A KV speedup is not automatically an NDNSF speedup.
\subsection{Representative Collaboration: Multi-Provider Inference}
A planner combines a supported model description with runtime ACK capabilities, assigns Providers, and prepares their model fragments.
Pipeline partitioning assigns sequential layers or layer groups.
Tensor partitioning divides operations or tensors and requires the corresponding collective exchanges.
Providers exchange activations or collective inputs over declared dependencies.
ONNX~\cite{onnx} describes the computation graph; export alone does not implement cross-Provider collectives or establish numerical correctness.
Model partitioning has substantial prior work~\cite{neurosurgeon,ddnn}; the NDNSF question concerns runtime assignment and authorized named-data execution.
Autoregressive generation also uses each generated token in a later decoding step.
This temporal dependency differs from forward computation through the layers.
The evaluation separates model preparation, prefill, time to first token, subsequent decoding, state storage, and data transfer.
Claims remain specific to tested models, precisions, partitions, and devices.
A feasible single-Provider baseline is retained; if a model cannot fit one device, distributed feasibility is meaningful but a speedup against a non-running baseline is not.

\chapter{Conclusion}
The research builds on NDNSF's initial ability to discover multiple candidates and select one Provider for an invocation.
It evaluates that discovery/authorization foundation and investigates an extension for complementary Provider roles and named dependencies.
The intended contribution is an evaluated service protocol and design rationale, not a new encryption primitive or the first use of named computation.
RQ1 compares ABE-backed authorization with DNMP-inspired role rules paired with content encryption, including their management and withdrawal costs.
RQ2 asks how runtime assignments become local rules for accepting named dependencies.
RQ3 examines benefits and costs for invocation and collaboration separately.
Existing campaigns establish limited invocation findings; the collaboration and cross-application claims still require their declared end-to-end evidence.
This separation provides a concrete route from the present proposal to a defensible dissertation.
\subsection{Rationale for ABE-Backed Service Authorization}
NDNSF uses ABE to protect discovery descriptors and reuses attribute-based service permissions in its invocation checks.
The first choice addresses confidentiality before the participating Providers are known; the second keeps service entitlements independent of identity-signing credentials.
Neither implies that ABE is always preferable to role-based authorization with suitable encryption.
Withdrawal and rekeying are lifecycle costs to evaluate.
Execution authorization determines whether a User may invoke a service; Provider authorization determines whether an entity may offer that service.
Content confidentiality limits who can read protected content.
The Controller administers these service permissions; the User and Provider check them during invocation.
Signature validation under trust rules and invocation-state checks remain necessary.
Permission to offer a service is distinct from selection for one particular task.

The design addresses three requirements: keep discovery descriptors non-public before participating Providers are identified; authenticate participants, verify their service permissions, and reject replayed invocation messages; and support permission grants and withdrawals during operation.
Permission aggregation is an additional management benefit, not a fourth security guarantee.

\subsection{Authorization Mechanisms, Lifecycle, and Costs}
\paragraph{Identity authentication.}
The User and Provider validate Data signatures and certificate chains under the applicable trust rules.
This identifies an accepted signer; it does not alone establish that signer's permission to offer or invoke the requested service.
\paragraph{Service-permission verification.}
In the ABE-backed invocation path, the User generates a fresh random value, \emph{RequestNonce}, and includes it in ABE-protected Request content.
This is an NDNSF application-level value, not the NDN Interest Nonce.
A Provider that recovers it returns it in ACK Data; the User compares the returned value with the one stored for the active request.
Thus RequestNonce supports both request binding and a check of access to the service-protected value.
The Provider generates \emph{ProviderChallenge} and includes it in ABE-protected ACK content.
The User uses the recovered ProviderChallenge to construct Selection Data.
Before execution, the Provider validates Selection Data using ProviderChallenge stored for that request.
Together with current service-permission checks, these checks determine whether the Provider may offer the service and whether the User may invoke it.
These checks demonstrate access to protected challenge values, not the creation of new permissions or a formal proof of exclusive key possession.
Authorized key or challenge sharing is outside the claimed threat protection.
This reuses attribute-based permission management rather than a separate set of role-based invocation rules.
It is not cost-free: confidential discovery already needs Provider DKEYs, whereas User permission DKEYs and challenge processing are additional authorization costs.
ABE confidentiality combined with DNMP-inspired role authorization remains a valid alternative.
\paragraph{Replay protection.}
Participants match messages to an active request and its protocol state.
The Provider records whether ProviderChallenge has already been used to accept Selection Data for execution; receiving the same Selection again must not start another execution.
This requires appropriate retention and invalidation of request state, including across restart.
Neither encryption nor possession of a challenge value alone prevents replay.
These admission checks do not establish exactly-once application side effects across crashes.
\paragraph{Runtime permission grants and withdrawals.}
The Controller updates permission status for both operations.
An ordinary grant updates the target entity's complete permission policy; that entity retrieves a replacement DKEY without changing the ABE public parameters.
Withdrawal additionally rotates the Controller's ABE master key and public parameters.
Entities retaining permissions obtain replacement DKEYs encoding their remaining permissions.
The master key stays with the Controller.
Rotation is Controller-wide, not confined to the withdrawn service.
In the revised dissemination design, the Controller publishes updated public parameters as signed named Data and uses Sync to announce their availability.
Participants retrieve and validate the parameters and Controller-signed \texttt{PolicyStatusData}, then refresh their DKEYs as required.
Ordinary grants also require participants to discover and retrieve updated permission status, even though the public parameters have not changed.
Sync is an update-discovery mechanism, not the authority for granting permission.
The local implementation supports status retrieval and parameter rotation; the dedicated Sync announcement path remains to be verified end to end.
Current-permission checks enforce withdrawal after the updated status has been retrieved and validated.
Parameter rotation restricts exchanges encrypted under the new generation.
Disconnected nodes cannot apply updates immediately, and previously disclosed keys or plaintext cannot be taken back.
\paragraph{Lifecycle comparison and evaluation.}
DNMP specifies validity bounds and replay-state handling~\cite{dnmp}; these do not by themselves provide immediate withdrawal of an unexpired role key.
For the comparison, a DNMP-inspired design can revoke the relevant credential and require execution nodes to check signed revocation status or reject expired certificates.
This invalidates authority at the validator; it does not physically retrieve distributed certificates.
Both approaches require update propagation, and neither retracts previously disclosed keys or plaintext.
Focused integration tests exercise NDNSF's runtime revocation checks, including identity-, certificate-, and service-scoped withdrawal.
These tests establish behavior at the exercised runtime boundaries, not network-wide instantaneous revocation or lower cost than certificate-based alternatives.
The remaining evaluation should measure status-propagation delay, rejection delay, rekeying traffic, and effects on unaffected members.
Runtime status validation and key rotation support runtime permission changes, with explicit propagation and rekeying costs.
They are not ABE-exclusive capabilities.

NDNSF introduces ABE for confidential discovery and reuses its service-permission management for invocation checks and permission updates; signatures and request-state checks remain necessary, separate parts of the design.

\section{论点与研究问题}
拟验证的论点是：命名且可验证的对象能够支持运行时服务发现和获准的单 Provider 调用，而明确的角色与依赖规则能够将这一基础扩展到多 Provider 任务。
研究分别评估发现／授权设计和协作扩展。
收益必须在所测条件下足以说明发现、验证、通信与密钥管理成本的合理性。
\item NDNSF 如何发现愿意参与的 Provider，同时避免未获准者读取发现描述，并在执行前检查服务权限？相对完整替代设计，其成本是什么？
\item 如何扩展单 Provider 调用基础，让运行时选定的多个 Provider 按任务角色和命名依赖执行，而不依赖中间 Data 来自生产者还是缓存？
\item 在何种任务和网络条件下，这些机制改善完成率、时延或执行效率？何时成本超过收益？
RQ1 评价调用基础，包括适配到 NDNSF 流程的 DNMP-inspired 角色授权加内容加密对照；RQ2 通过 UAV／DI 依赖检验协作扩展；RQ3 分别测量两者及其失败行为。
\section{贡献与证据边界}
预期贡献是经评价的发现／授权设计、通过命名依赖检查落实运行时分工的协作协议，以及收益和成本证据；研究基于已有 NDN、加密与计算机制。
已有调用实验不验证多角色计划。
扩展新增角色与依赖规则，不替代已有 request ID 隔离。
后续实现不归为初版能力；协作端到端评价仍未完成。
“已有证据与待完成评价”章区分现有结论和待补证据。

\section{授权与保密性}
发现 descriptor 的保密范围是缺少相应 ABE 解密能力的实体，不排除其他获准候选，也不隐藏流量。
在请求级保护设计中，User 用对称密钥加密应用输入，并通过 Selection 交付所需密钥材料；这些材料加密给经过认证的选定 Provider 公钥。
响应密钥由请求方 User 和选定 Provider 共享。
其他 User 在密钥未泄露的假设下不能解密结果；生成结果的 Provider 必然知道明文。
这里定义被评估设计的保护要求，而非所有历史实现路径的行为。

\section{命名对象准入与恢复}
按拟议准入规则，下游 Provider 接受依赖前先检查执行仍然活动且未超出截止时间，再验证信任规则下的 Data 签名、当前请求／计划／执行身份、指定前驱生产者，以及声明边允许的名字／数据格式／密钥范围。

生产者、缓存和仓库获取执行相同检查。
计划引用实际生产者授权命名空间中的对象，而不以其他生产者身份重新发布。
\caption{拟议状态约束及所需反例，不代表全部生产路径已验收。}
\toprule 状态／事件 & 规则\\\midrule
收集 ACK & 窗口关闭后迟到 ACK 不静默修改已提交计划\\\midrule
收到 Selection & 身份、challenge、授权和资源检查通过才开始；ACK 本身不启动任务\\\midrule
等待依赖 & 所需合法边满足才推进；错误角色、边、对象或执行身份必须拒绝\\\midrule
完成／取消 & 重复消息按已记录状态处理，不隐式重复副作用\\\midrule
失败／重分配 & 显式终止或新授权；旧执行不能获得新分配的权限，结果复用必须被明确允许\\\bottomrule
网络重取不等于重新计算。
取消、旧执行隔离及结果复用须有明确规则；缓存对象是否可用取决于新计划授权。
补偿不提供分布式原子事务或物理操作 exactly-once。
RQ1、RQ2 分别需要授权比较和计划／状态测试；设计描述及已有调用实验不能替代协作验证。
\section{有条件的正确性论证}
假定签名密钥安全、信任／授权检查正确、Provider 遵守状态机：全部启动路径须核验活动 Selection 及未使用的一次性授权状态；全部输入路径（含缓存）须核验指定生产者和声明边。
重分配须隔离旧 worker 和迟到回调。
重启须保留相关状态或使其安全失效；签名和 FreshnessPeriod 不能替代这些检查。
这些是有条件的不变量和实现论证义务，不是完整系统的密码学证明。
反例应包括同请求错误角色、合法签名生产者提供未声明边、重分配后迟到回调，分别检验 request ID 本身不表达的性质。
应用结果语义及物理副作用仍不属于该论证。

\section{NDNSF-UAV：控制、感知与协作}
\subsection{应用结构与服务流程}
UAV 应用连接操作员地面站与无人机侧服务容器。
无人机通过 NDNSF 暴露相机操作、遥测和任务相关服务；地面站也可以提供目标检测服务，因此同一应用包含服务消费与服务提供两类行为。
应用解释相机、飞行器和任务数据，NDNSF 提供可复用的调用与数据交付机制。
这些操作检验不同的框架要求：选择当前可用的感知 Provider 检验发现与 ACK 选择；控制已选定的飞行器检验与该 Provider 关联的调用，而不是任意替换执行者。
遥测和任务状态获取检验返回 Data 与目标飞行器及活动操作的关联。
长任务为取消、截止时间和迟到状态提供验证场景。
测试必须区分拒绝非法命令与飞控实际执行获准命令。
直播和录制使用不同的数据路径。
相机 Start/Stop 是服务控制操作，随后直播使用命名数据流接口；录制引用与完整存储对象则需要精确对象获取，不能依赖缓存必然持久保存。
这些功能因此可以检验流生命周期、顺序和缺口处理、内容保护及数据产品获取。
编解码、图像处理、操作界面和飞行安全仍由应用负责，但它们对 NDNSF 的使用同样属于框架验证范围。

units.latex: \section{NDNSF-DI：推理生命周期、状态与协作}
\subsection{应用结构与推理流程}
NDNSF-DI 是框架之上的推理应用层，解释模型和任务描述，组织模型准备与执行，并向调用方提供结果。
原生请求方与 Provider 接口包含请求提交、服务注册、结果／事件处理和取消，会话相关接口还携带续接状态。
接口存在并不表示所有模型或恢复配置都已通过端到端测试。
单 Provider 推理不需要模型切分，也可以检验服务发现、权限检查、选择、受保护输入交付与结果获取。
冷模型准备与驻留模型复用检验不同的就绪和模型文件访问路径。
模型文件等对象可使用受管理的 Repo 存储；Content Store 仍是机会缓存，不保证持久保存。
DI 定义模型身份、兼容性与放置策略，NDNSF 提供服务生命周期及命名对象交换。
流式推理与会话流程将验证扩展到增量输出、取消、终态和请求特定状态。
模型权重、activation 与 key/value（K/V）状态具有不同生命周期。
模型计算 K/V 张量，推理运行时保留它们用于后续解码；共享缓冲区可避免每步复制整个 cache~\cite{ortkvcache}，但权重驻留不能替代这些状态。
DI 负责分词和 KV 兼容规则，框架验证关注应用使用这些状态时所经过的授权请求、数据交换与生命周期。
KV 加速并不自动等于 NDNSF 加速。

\chapter{研究计划与决策门}
先固定一个 UAV 图和一个支持的 DI 切分，形成可运行和可验证基线，而不是完成所有开发功能。
tensor/hybrid、LLM 流式和复杂恢复只有证据足够才保留为最终主张。
负面性能结果在条件清楚时也是有效研究结论。

\chapter{结论}
本研究以初版 NDNSF 从多个候选中选定一个 Provider 完成调用的能力为基础，评价发现／授权设计，并研究面向互补角色和命名依赖的协作扩展。
候选贡献是经评价的服务协议及有证据支持的机制选择，不是新密码学原语或首次命名计算。
RQ1 比较 ABE-backed 授权与 DNMP-inspired 角色规则配合内容加密，纳入管理和撤销成本；RQ2 把运行时分工变成本地命名依赖准入规则；RQ3 分别评价调用与协作的收益和成本。
已有实验支持有限调用结论；协作与跨应用主张仍需其声明的端到端证据。

units.section_or_title: 采用 ABE-backed 服务授权的理由
units.latex: NDNSF 使用 ABE 保护发现描述，并在调用检查中复用基于属性的服务权限。

units.section_or_title: 采用 ABE-backed 服务授权的理由
units.latex: 前者解决具体参与者尚未确定时的内容保密问题；后者让服务权限与身份签名凭证 分离管理。

units.section_or_title: 采用 ABE-backed 服务授权的理由
units.latex: 这不意味着 ABE 总优于角色授权配合适当加密；撤销和换钥仍是需要 评估的生命周期成本。

units.section_or_title: 采用 ABE-backed 服务授权的理由
units.latex: 执行授权决定 User 是否可以调用服务， Provider 授权决定实体是否可以提供该服务；内容机密性限制谁能读取受保护内容。

units.section_or_title: 采用 ABE-backed 服务授权的理由
units.latex: Controller 管理服务权限，User 和 Provider 在调用过程中检查这些权限，并执行 信任规则下的签名验证与调用状态检查。

units.section_or_title: 采用 ABE-backed 服务授权的理由
units.latex: 获准提供服务不等于被选中执行某一次任务。

units.section_or_title: 采用 ABE-backed 服务授权的理由
units.latex: 该设计面向三个要求：参与 Provider 尚未确定时不公开发现描述；认证参与者身份、 验证服务权限并拒绝重放调用消息；运行时授予和撤销服务权限。

units.section_or_title: 采用 ABE-backed 服务授权的理由
units.latex: 权限聚合是额外的 管理便利，而不是第四项安全保证。

units.latex: DNMP 则通过角色签名密钥与 Trust Schema 约束命令目标和动作~\cite{dnmp}。

units.latex: \subsection{授权机制、生命周期与成本}
\paragraph{身份认证。}
User 和 Provider 按适用的信任规则验证 Data 签名与证书链。
这确定了被接受的 签名身份，但单独不能确定该身份是否有权提供或调用所请求的服务。
\paragraph{服务权限验证。}
在 ABE-backed 调用路径中，User 为请求生成新的随机值 \emph{RequestNonce}， 并将其放入 ABE 保护的 Request 内容。
这是 NDNSF 应用层的值， 不是 NDN Interest 的 Nonce。
Provider 恢复该值后在 ACK Data 中返回， User 将返回值与活动请求中保存的值比较。
因此，RequestNonce 既用于请求绑定， 也用于检查对方能否获取该服务保护的值。
Provider 生成 \emph{ProviderChallenge}， 并将其放入 ABE 保护的 ACK 内容。
User 使用恢复出的 ProviderChallenge 构造 Selection Data。
执行前，Provider 使用为该请求保存的 ProviderChallenge 验证 Selection Data。
这些检查结合当前服务权限检查，确定 Provider 能否提供该服务， 以及 User 能否调用该服务。
这些检查表明参与者能够获得受保护的 challenge 值，不会创建新权限，也不是 密钥独占持有的形式化证明。
获准实体主动共享密钥或 challenge 不在所声称的 防护范围内。

\paragraph{生命周期对比与评估。}
DNMP 规定了有效期约束与防重放状态处理~\cite{dnmp}；这些机制本身不等于立即 撤销尚未过期的角色密钥。
作为对照设计，DNMP-inspired 方案可以撤销相关凭证， 并要求执行节点检查签名的撤销状态或拒绝过期证书。
这是在验证方取消凭证 所代表的权限，而不是物理取回已分发的证书。
两类方案都需要传播更新信息， 也都无法收回已披露的密钥或明文。
定向集成测试已检验 NDNSF 的运行时撤销检查，包括身份级、证书级和服务级 撤销。
这些测试支持已覆盖运行时边界上的行为，不代表整个网络中的瞬时撤销， 也不能证明其成本低于证书方案。
后续评估应测量状态传播延迟、拒绝生效延迟、 重新分发密钥的流量，以及对未撤销成员的影响。
因此，运行时状态验证和密钥 轮换支持运行时权限变更，同时带来明确的状态传播和重新分发密钥的成本。
这些并非 ABE 独有能力。
NDNSF 为保密发现引入 ABE，并复用其服务权限管理 进行调用检查和权限更新；签名验证与请求状态检查仍是独立且必要的设计组成。

units.latex: \begin{frame}{Three Security Requirements; One Additional Benefit}

units.section_or_title: Three Security Requirements; One Additional Benefit
units.latex: \item Keep discovery descriptors non-public before participating Providers are identified.

units.section_or_title: Three Security Requirements; One Additional Benefit

units.latex: \vspace{3mm}\bluebox{Additional benefit: aggregate service permissions in a decryption key (DKEY) while retaining identity-signing credentials. This is a management property, not another security guarantee.}
\begin{frame}{Reason 1: Confidential Discovery Before Selection}
\item The User knows the service, but not yet the currently willing Provider identities.
\item An observation area and deadline can reveal intended activity even without the full application input.
\item The User encrypts the descriptor using ABE and the service attribute, without listing Provider identities. [19]
\vspace{3mm}\bluebox{Confidential from parties lacking the required decryption capability. Authorized but unselected Providers can read it; names and traffic patterns remain visible.}
\begin{frame}{Reason 2: Reuse Service-Permission Management}
\item ABE was introduced to keep discovery descriptors non-public. [19]
\item NDNSF reuses the attribute authority to manage Provider and User service permissions. [28]
\item RequestNonce and ProviderChallenge checks use these permissions during invocation.

\vspace{3mm}\bluebox{ABE discovery plus role-based invocation is also possible. NDNSF avoids adding role signing credentials solely for service membership; signature validation and request-state checks remain necessary. User DKEYs and challenge processing still add cost.}
\begin{frame}{How NDNSF Checks Service Permissions}
\item Provider permission: recover RequestNonce from ABE-protected Request content and return it in ACK Data. The User compares it with RequestNonce stored for this request.
\item User permission: recover ProviderChallenge from ABE-protected ACK content and construct Selection Data. The Provider validates Selection using its stored ProviderChallenge.
\vspace{3mm}\bluebox{Also check current service permissions. These checks show access to protected values, not exclusive key possession. RequestNonce is not the Interest Nonce.}

\begin{frame}{Additional Benefit: Aggregate Service Permissions}
\item Within one Controller domain, combine several service permissions in one entity's DKEY; retain identity-signing credentials. [19,28]
\item DNMP represents command authority through role keys and schema rules. One role can permit several commands. [12]
\item Where equivalent permissions require distinct role credentials, NDNSF avoids maintaining those extra signing credentials.
\vspace{3mm}\bluebox{Fewer independently managed credentials does not imply fixed DKEY size or lower total cost. Policy size, key distribution and updates still matter.}
\begin{frame}{DNMP: Trust-Schema Command Authorization}
Distributed Network Measurement Protocol (DNMP) [12] authorizes measurement commands:
\item The Network Key anchors role keys, device keys, and the schema.
\item The client uses target, probe type, arguments, and user role to find an allowed signing key; among matching keys, it chooses the least privileged.
\item The receiving Network Observer Daemon validates the publication under the schema before dispatching the probe.

\vspace{2mm}\bluebox{DNMP also uses publication lifetimes and retained state against replay, assuming loosely synchronized clocks. These are concrete command-authorization mechanisms, not just identity checks.}
\begin{frame}{DNMP-inspired Authorization versus NDNSF}
\toprule Design & Execution authorization & Discovery confidentiality\\\midrule
DNMP-inspired [12] & Check role-constrained signatures and NDNSF invocation state & Pair with service-group encryption or ABE\\\midrule
NDNSF ABE-backed & Check signatures, RequestNonce, ProviderChallenge, current permissions and request state & User encrypts descriptor content with service-level ABE\\\bottomrule

\vspace{3mm}\bluebox{Proposed comparison: retain NDNSF discovery and Selection, with input/result protection and revocation checks in both designs. Trust Schema [16] alone does not encrypt Content; adapting DNMP authorization is not an original DNMP feature. No measured cost advantage is claimed.}

\begin{frame}{Runtime Permission Grants and Withdrawals}
\item Both operations update Controller-signed permission status. [28]
\item Ordinary grant: update the target's complete policy; it retrieves a replacement DKEY. Public parameters stay unchanged.
\item Withdrawal: rotate the Controller's ABE master key and public parameters; remaining members obtain DKEYs for their remaining permissions.

\vspace{3mm}\bluebox{The master key stays with the Controller. Rotation is Controller-wide. Participants must retrieve and validate updates before applying them; disconnected nodes cannot do so immediately.}

\begin{frame}{Threat Model: What Is Trusted?}
\item Trusted: Controller authorization and the User's planning decision.
\item Untrusted delivery: an object may arrive through a producer, forwarder, cache, or repository and still requires validation.
\item Adversarial cases to test: wrong identities, permissions, challenges, request state, roles, dependencies, or execution identities.
\item Not established by signatures/ABE: honest resource reports, correct inference, truthful images, or resistance to authorized key sharing.

\begin{frame}{Plan-to-Data Enforcement: Check Before Advancing}
\item Validate the Data signature using the appropriate trust rules.
\item Check active request, plan, execution identity and deadline.
\item Verify that the signer is the assigned predecessor Provider.
\item Check that the object matches the declared edge, permitted name, data format and key scope.
\item Require complete validated input before the dependent computation starts.
\vspace{3mm}\bluebox{Apply the same rules to direct, cached and repository-fetched Data. This is a proposed acceptance contract; full end-to-end qualification remains required.}
\begin{frame}{Collaboration Recovery Needs Explicit State}
\toprule Event & Required behavior\\\midrule
Late ACK & Do not silently change the committed plan\\\midrule
Duplicate Selection & Follow recorded one-time state; do not implicitly repeat a side effect\\\midrule
Incomplete dependency & Wait within policy/deadline, recover, or fail; do not execute on partial data\\\midrule
Provider replacement & Authorize a new assignment; reject old execution actions and specify permitted result reuse\\\midrule
Cancellation & Prevent late messages from reauthorizing cancelled work\\\bottomrule
\vspace{3mm}\bluebox{Network re-retrieval is not task re-execution. Compensation is not an atomic transaction or exactly-once physical action.}

\begin{frame}{DI State and Evidence Boundaries}
\item Model weights, reusable artifacts, request activations and KV state have different lifetimes.
\item With KV caching, the runtime reuses prior key/value (K/V) tensors and supplies next-step inputs; resident weights do not replace this state. [31]
\item An in-process test does not establish correct execution across processes or devices.
\item Freeze one supported model/partition first; tensor/hybrid and LLM streaming need their own evidence if claimed.
\vspace{3mm}\bluebox{Earlier small-model measurements do not validate the newer distributed inference and recovery paths. [28]}

\begin{frame}{Expected Research Outcomes}
\item \textbf{RQ1 answer:} when ABE-backed authorization is preferable to DNMP-inspired role rules plus encryption, accounting for confidentiality, management and withdrawal costs.
\item \textbf{RQ2 answer:} exactly which task-assignment mistakes are rejected and which recovery behavior is supported.
\item \textbf{RQ3 answer:} measured benefits, negative results and deployment limits.
\item Reproducible configurations and evidence linking each conclusion to its tested scope.
\bluebox{The outcome is a tested service protocol and an evidence-backed account of when its mechanisms are worth their cost.}
